content: 1. Orrell C et al. conducted a study on the conservation of first-line antiretroviral treatment regimens in settings where therapeutic options are limited. The findings were published in Antiviral Therapy in 2007, volume 12, pages 83–88. 2. Mermin J et al. evaluated the utility of routine viral load testing, CD4 cell counts, and clinical monitoring among adults with HIV receiving antiretroviral therapy in Uganda. This randomized trial was published in BMJ in 2011, volume 343, article d6792. 3. Jourdain G et al. compared CD4-based versus viral load-based ART monitoring and switching strategies in Thailand through the PHPT-3 randomized clinical trial. The study was accessed on May 15, 2013. 4. Saag MS et al. conducted a cluster-randomized trial in Zambia to compare routine versus discretionary viral load monitoring among adults initiating ART. The findings were presented at the 19th Annual Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections and accessed on May 15, 2013. 5. Keiser O et al. assessed the accuracy of WHO CD4 cell count criteria for detecting virological failure in antiretroviral therapy. The results were published in Tropical Medicine and International Health in 2009, volume 14, pages 1220–1225. 6. Abouyannis M et al. developed and validated systems for the rational use of viral load testing in adults receiving first-line ART in sub-Saharan Africa. The study was published in AIDS in 2011, volume 25, pages 1627–1635. 7. Chaiwarith R et al. investigated the sensitivity and specificity of CD4+ measurements and clinical evaluations in determining ART failure in Thailand. The findings were published in the International Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2007, volume 11, pages 413–416. 8. Hosseinipour M et al. validated clinical and immunological definitions of ART failure in Malawi. The study was accessed on May 15, 2013. 9. Kantor R et al. highlighted the misclassification of first-line ART failure based on immunological monitoring in resource-limited settings. The study was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2009, volume 49, pages 454–462. 10. Labhardt ND et al. developed a clinical prediction score to complement WHO criteria for ART failure in resource-limited settings, based on experience from Lesotho. The study was published in PLoS ONE in 2012, volume 7, article e47937. 11. Mee P et al. evaluated WHO criteria for ART failure in resource-limited settings, with a focus on South Africa. The findings were published in AIDS in 2008, volume 22, pages 1971–1977. 12. Meya D et al. developed and evaluated a clinical algorithm for monitoring patients on ART in resource-limited settings using adherence, clinical, and CD4 cell count criteria. The study was published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society in 2009, volume 12, article 3. 13. Moore DM et al. demonstrated that CD4+ T-cell count monitoring does not accurately identify virological failure in HIV-infected adults on ART. The study was published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2008, volume 49, pages 477–484. 14. Rawizza H et al. found that immunological criteria are poor predictors of virological outcomes, with implications for HIV treatment monitoring in resource-limited settings. The study was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2011, volume 53, pages 1283–1290. 15. Rewari BB evaluated the role of targeted viral load testing in assessing patients for second-line ART in India. The study was published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2010, volume 55, pages 610–614. 16. Reynolds SJ et al. reported the failure of immunological criteria to appropriately identify ART failure in Uganda. The study was published in AIDS in 2009, volume 23, pages 697–700. 17. Van Oosterhout JJ et al. assessed the poor performance of clinical and immunological WHO criteria in diagnosing ART failure in Malawi. The study was published in Tropical Medicine and International Health in 2009, volume 14, pages 856–861. 18. Barlow-Mosha L et al. validated WHO 2010 immunological criteria for predicting pediatric first-line ART failure in Uganda, concluding that CD4 is a poor surrogate for virological monitoring. The study was accessed on May 15, 2013. 19. Davies M-A et al. examined the accuracy of immunological criteria for identifying virological failure in children on ART in the IeDEA Southern Africa Collaboration. The study was published in Tropical Medicine and International Health in 2011, volume 16, pages 1367–1371. 20. Davies M-A et al. explored the role of targeted viral load testing in diagnosing virological failure in children on ART with immunological failure. The study was published ahead of print. 21. Westley BP et al. evaluated the 2010 WHO guidelines for predicting treatment failures in Cambodian children with HIV, finding high misclassification rates and drug resistance. The study was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2012, volume 55, pages 432–440. 22. Laurent C et al. compared monitoring strategies for ART in rural Cameroon, including viral load, CD4 counts, and clinical assessments versus clinical monitoring alone. The study was published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2011, volume 11, pages 825–833. 23. Mugyenyi P et al. conducted the DART trial to compare routine versus clinically driven laboratory monitoring of ART in Africa. The study was published in The Lancet in 2010, volume 375, pages 123–131. 24. Havlir DV et al. investigated the prevalence and predictive value of intermittent viremia in patients on combination HIV therapy. The study was published in JAMA in 2001, volume 286, pages 171–179. 25. Mocroft A et al. assessed the safety of discontinuing primary Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis in virologically suppressed HIV patients with CD4 counts below 200 cells/μL. The study was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2010, volume 51, pages 611–619. 26. Gale HB et al. questioned the necessity of frequent CD4+ T-lymphocyte count monitoring in patients with counts ≥300 cells/μL and HIV-1 suppression. The study was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases. 27. Johannessen A et al. demonstrated the effectiveness of dried blood spots for viral load monitoring in patients on ART in rural Tanzania. The study was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2009, volume 49, pages 976–981.
